segments.say: Welcome. Find a comfortable spot, maybe dim the lights a little, because tonight we're going to spend some unhurried time with a question almost everyone asks at some point. Can a person really change? Not just a new haircut or a new routine for a week, but who they are underneath. Your temper, your shyness, your habits, the way you react when things go wrong.

You probably know the moment I mean. It's the first of January, or the start of a new month, or the morning after a hard week. You decide that this time will be different. You'll be calmer, braver, more organised, kinder to yourself. And then, a few weeks later, you catch yourself doing the old thing again, and a quiet voice says, see, this is just who you are.

In the first half, we'll look at what the research actually says, with named studies and the doubts left in. In the second half, the pace will slow right down into a gentle wind-down, so if you drift off along the way, that's perfectly fine. That's what this is for.

segments.say: So let's take that quiet voice seriously for a moment. The one that says, this is just who you are. Is it right? Is personality fixed, the way eye colour is fixed? Or is it something softer, something that moves with time and effort? Psychologists have argued about this for more than a century, and the answer turns out to be more interesting than either side expected.

Let's begin with one of the most famous sentences ever written about character. It comes from William James, the American philosopher and psychologist, in his huge book The Principles of Psychology, published in 1890.

James wrote this in his chapter on habit. He wasn't being gloomy for the sake of it. He was making a point about how much of our lives runs on routines we built when we were young. Once those routines are laid down, he argued, they carry us along, whether we like them or not.

show.text: In most of us, by the age of thirty, the character has set like plaster, and will never soften again.
show.by: William James, The Principles of Psychology, 1890

segments.say: It's a powerful image, isn't it? Wet plaster can be shaped. Dry plaster can only be broken. And for most of the twentieth century, a version of this idea was taken seriously by many personality researchers. The thinking went like this. Children and teenagers are still forming. But by early adulthood, the basic shape of a person is done.

To test an idea like that, you first need a way to measure personality. Over the twentieth century, researchers settled on a set of five broad traits that show up again and again in questionnaires across many countries. They're often called the Big Five.

Openness is about curiosity, imagination and a taste for new experiences. Conscientiousness is about being organised, reliable and self-disciplined. Extraversion is about how much energy you get from other people. Agreeableness is warmth and cooperation. And neuroticism, which some researchers prefer to call low emotional stability, is about how strongly you tend to feel worry, sadness and stress.

show.title: The Big Five traits
items: Openness: curiosity and love of new ideas
Extraversion: sociability and energy around others
Neuroticism: how strongly you feel worry and stress

segments.say: None of these are boxes you're either in or out of. Each one is more like a dial, and most people sit somewhere in the middle. With these five dials, researchers could ask a clear question. If we measure the same people years apart, do the dials stay where they were?

The best way to answer that is with longitudinal studies, which follow the same people over many years. One study of this kind is useful. Dozens are much better. So in 2006, Brent Roberts, Kate Walton and Wolfgang Viechtbauer gathered them together.

They combined the results of ninety-two longitudinal studies, covering people from adolescence into old age. Instead of asking whether one person changed, they asked how the average person changed over the years. If James was right, the lines should go flat after thirty.

show.what: Patterns of mean-level change in personality traits across the life course: a meta-analysis of longitudinal studies

segments.say: They didn't go flat. People, on average, kept changing well past thirty. And the direction of the change was remarkably consistent. As people moved through adulthood, they tended to become more conscientious, more emotionally stable, and in some ways more socially confident. Agreeableness also tended to rise, especially later in life.

Interestingly, the biggest changes didn't happen in adolescence, as many people had assumed. Much of the change happened in young adulthood, roughly between twenty and forty. That's the stretch of life when many people take on new roles, like steady work, long relationships and caring for others.

Researchers have a name for this pattern. They call it the maturity principle. Over time, most people tend to grow into calmer, more responsible and more caring versions of themselves. Not everyone, and not in a straight line, but on average, that's the drift.

show.sub: Growing into steadier versions of ourselves

segments.say: One meta-analysis is strong evidence. But here's another angle on the same question, from a very large sample collected in a very modern way.

In 2003, Sanjay Srivastava and his colleagues published a study using personality questionnaires completed online by more than a hundred and thirty-two thousand adults, aged twenty-one to sixty. Notice the title they chose. Set like plaster, or persistent change? They were testing William James directly.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2003
show.what: Development of personality in early and middle adulthood: set like plaster or persistent change?

segments.say: This was not a longitudinal study. It compared people of different ages at one moment in time, which has limits. But the pattern was clear and it matched the long studies. Conscientiousness and agreeableness kept rising through the twenties, thirties and beyond. Neuroticism tended to fall, especially in women. The plaster, it seemed, was still soft.

Now, there's a subtle point here that's worth slowing down for. Researchers talk about two different kinds of stability. One is about the average level. Do people in general become more conscientious over time? The other is about rank order. Does the most organised person in a group of twenty-year-olds tend to still be among the most organised at fifty?

And here's the thing. Both can be true at once. Imagine a group of runners all moving forward along a track. Everyone is going somewhere new, but the runner in front often stays near the front. That's roughly what personality looks like in adulthood. The whole group moves, and individual positions shift a little, but slowly.

So William James was partly right. Habits and routines do carry us. But the idea that character sets solid at thirty, never to soften again, doesn't hold up. Personality keeps moving, slowly, for most of our lives.

show.cap: A slow drift over many years

segments.say: And yet, if personality really keeps changing, why does it feel so fixed from the inside? Why do so many of us believe that the person we are today is, more or less, the person we'll always be? That's where we're going next, because psychologists have measured that feeling too. And it turns out to be one of the most reliable illusions they've ever found.
